title: Ender and sustainer of all
hook: sarab kaal hain, sarab paal hain: He ends all and He sustains all (Jaap)

segments.voice: Yesterday, one form, seen in countless ways, and your line, one, seen many ways. Today, two words that sound like opposites, held by one hand.

Walk through a forest in late autumn. The leaves are coming down, thousands of them, every one a small ending. Kick through them, and underneath is dark, crumbly soil: last year's leaves, already turning into food for the tree that dropped them. The same tree is letting go and being fed, at once, by the same falling. A gardener knows this. So does anyone who has sat in a hospital where one family grieves down the hall from another holding a newborn. Endings and keepings sit close together, and Jaap Sahib puts them in one breath.
screen: `AUTUMN LEAVES COMING DOWN.` → `LAST YEAR'S LEAVES FEED THE TREE.` → `ENDINGS AND KEEPINGS, CLOSE TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: The words are sarab kaal and sarab paal. Sarab means all. Kaal you met eleven days ago: time, and death, the thing that ends. Paal is the root of paalna, the Punjabi word for raising a child: feeding, protecting, keeping alive. So Jaap salutes the One as the ending of all things and the keeping of all things. Now set this beside the glide's first word. On day three hundred thirty-seven, Jaap bowed to akaal, the One without kaal. Here the same One is called the kaal of everything. A contradiction? Not as Sikh scripture reads it. In Sikh teaching, the One isn't subject to time, but every ending in time happens within the One's order, which Sikhs call hukam. Guru Nanak's Japji says everything is within hukam, and nothing is outside it: births, deaths, harvests, partings. The Tenth Guru is willing to use the hard name too. Elsewhere in his writing he speaks of the One as Kaal and Mahakaal, great Time, the power that brings all things to their close. He doesn't pretend endings aren't real, or that they come from somewhere else. But here Jaap doesn't say sarab kaal alone; it comes with sarab paal. The hand that ends is the hand that keeps, as the leaf falls and the soil feeds the tree. For Sikhs living through an ending, that pairing can be a quiet comfort: in Jaap, the One who closes doors is also the One who keeps.
screen: `SARAB KAAL: THE ENDING OF ALL.` · `SARAB PAAL: THE KEEPING OF ALL.` · `HUKAM: NOTHING OUTSIDE THE ORDER.` · `THE HAND THAT ENDS ALSO KEEPS.` · then, large: `ENDS AND KEEPS.`

segments.voice: Think back over this week and find one thing that ended, a project, a season, a habit, a conversation, and hold it gently for a breath. Then find one thing that began, even something small, and hold that too, letting the two sit side by side without choosing between them. If you pray, you can place both in the same hand.
Sarab kaal. The ending of all — paired in Jaap with sarab paal, the keeping of all: the One who brings every ending and keeps every life, in one breath.
Your line: ends and keeps. The hand that ends is the same hand that keeps. Day three hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs understand births, deaths and every change as happening within hukam, the One's order, and recite Jaap's pairing of the One who ends and keeps all things each morning.
